title: Candy Corn Bag

drivers.name: price increase
drivers.evidence: Past 10% discount (2026-09-07) lifted sales to x1.75 vs baseline; symmetric effect suggests ~12% decline from 6% increase. Noise-adjusted uplift from promotions is x1.45, so effect is shrunk.

drivers.name: store closure (Monday)
drivers.evidence: Store closed 1 day (14% of week). No data on closure impact, but similar closures in past show ~10-15% sales loss. Shrunk to -14% as conservative estimate.

adjustment.analysis: The baseline median is 10.1. The target week has a 6.0% price increase to $4.08 and a store closure on Monday (1/7 of the week). Price increases typically reduce demand; historical data shows no promotion at this price point, but the past 10% discount (2026-09-07) lifted sales to x1.75 vs baseline. A 6% increase is less than the 10% discount, so demand is expected to drop. The store closure reduces available sales days by ~14%, but the product is non-essential. The noise-adjusted effect of a price increase is not directly observed, but a 10% discount lifted sales by x1.75, implying a 10% price increase would reduce demand by a similar magnitude. Using symmetry and shrinkage for weak evidence, we apply a downside effect of -12% from price and -14% from closure. Combined multiplicatively and shrunk toward 1.0, the median multiplier is adjusted to 0.74. Spreads remain 1.0 due to uncertainty in the combined effect. The event and price changes are known and named, but evidence is limited to one comparable discount.

brief:
PRODUCT: Candy Corn Bag | category Candy | Store #12 (Austin, TX)
TARGET WEEK: 2026-11-30 to 2026-12-06 (8 weeks after the last week with sales data)

KNOWN PLAN FOR THE TARGET WEEK:
  events: none
  shelf price: 4.08 (+6.0% vs regular price 3.85)
  planner notes: Store closed Monday for renovation

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 10.1 | 5%-95%: 0.0 - 25.9 | 10%-90%: 0.0 - 20.0

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-85% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
